John Calvin
JON KAL-vin
proper noun (Reformer, 1509–1564)
French Reformer; principal architect of the Reformed branch of the Reformation; author of the Institutes of the Christian Religion (first edition 1536, expanded through five editions to the definitive 1559 Latin edition). Pastor of Geneva (1536-1538; 1541-1564). The most influential single voice of the magisterial Reformation alongside Luther.

See also: John Calvin

📖 Biblical Definition

French Reformer (1509-1564) and principal architect of the Reformed branch of the Reformation. Born at Noyon in Picardy; trained in classical letters at Paris (Collège de la Marche, Collège de Montaigu), then in law at Orléans and Bourges. Converted to Reformation views around 1533; fled France in 1534 after the affair of the placards; published the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion at Basel in 1536; recruited by William Farel to remain in Geneva that same year. Calvin served two pastorates at Geneva (1536-1538; 1541-1564), with an exile in Strasbourg between (1538-1541) during which he pastored a French refugee congregation, married Idelette de Bure (1540), and produced his most important Pauline commentaries. Returning to Geneva at the council's invitation in 1541, Calvin labored for the rest of his life to establish a thoroughly reformed church-and-civil order: the Geneva Academy (founded 1559, ancestor of the University of Geneva); the Genevan Psalter (the great Reformed-confessional metrical Psalter); the Ecclesiastical Ordinances (1541) establishing the four-office structure (pastors, teachers, elders, deacons); and the steady refinement of the Institutes through five editions. Calvin's commentaries cover most of the Bible; his sermons (preserved in stenographic transcription) run to thousands; his pastoral correspondence shows the scope of his international labor. The patriarchal-Reformed reader receives Calvin as the great theological architect of the Reformed-confessional tradition whose work undergirds every subsequent Reformed development.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

French Reformer (1509-1564); principal architect of Reformed branch of Reformation; Institutes of the Christian Religion; pastor of Geneva (1536-1538; 1541-1564); founded Geneva Academy.

JOHN CALVIN, proper n. (1509-1564) French Reformer and principal architect of the Reformed branch of the Reformation. Born at Noyon in Picardy; trained in classical letters at Paris and in law at Orléans and Bourges. Converted c. 1533; fled France 1534; published the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion at Basel 1536. Recruited by Farel to Geneva. Two pastorates at Geneva (1536-1538; 1541-1564) with Strasbourg exile between (1538-1541). Established Geneva Academy (1559); the Genevan Psalter; the Ecclesiastical Ordinances (1541) with four-office church government. Final 1559 Latin edition of Institutes the definitive form. Hundreds of biblical commentaries; thousands of sermons; international pastoral correspondence. Married Idelette de Bure 1540.

2 Timothy 2:15 — "Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

No major postmodern redefinition. Calvin is universally received in the Reformed-confessional tradition; the principal contemporary mishandling is the caricature of Calvinism as Calvin's personal idiosyncrasy rather than as the integrated biblical-confessional tradition it shaped.

expand to see more

John Calvin as a proper name does not undergo lexical corruption. The principal contemporary mishandling is the popular-evangelical caricature of Calvinism as Calvin's personal idiosyncrasy — a particular angle of theological vision peculiar to one French reformer — rather than the integrated biblical-confessional tradition Calvin gave systematic form to but did not invent. Calvin's theology was substantively shared with Bucer, Bullinger, Vermigli, and the broader Reformed-magisterial tradition; his contribution was the supreme systematic and pastoral articulation. The patriarchal-Reformed reader receives Calvin as the great organizing voice of a tradition broader than himself, the Reformer whose Institutes remains a substantive theological resource five centuries later.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

French Reformer; Geneva; Institutes; Reformed-confessional tradition's architect.
